event_subtitle: Exhibition Title: Diagrams of Memory: Interwoven Ontology
description:
Camille Ann Brewer lives and works in the City of Detroit, Michigan.  Through the process of textile construction, Brewer’s artwork intersects cartographic and photographic images that speak to specific spaces and time. Weaving together of physical place, memory with time is the core subject of this body of work.  

The artwork is built with time-period paper maps, which illustrate spatial geography and political territory; along with paper-collaged images of people, places and things, which tie directly to the history and human relationships in space.  In patterns that support the artwork’s theme, the two disparate paper elements are then woven together to create a serendipitous making and aesthetic experience.

combined_title: Comics Beyond Sight
description:
This exhibit covers a variety of creative approaches to comics visual accessibility, and by extension visual accessibility broadly. Those approaches range from multimedia (audio and textual descriptions) through multidimensional and emerging technologies strategies (3D printing, haptics, and screen-based mobile touch interfaces). It demonstrates that comics can be made accessible. Learn about the international efforts of innovators in the realm of comics accessibility for those who are blind or have low vision, assembled by the Accessible Comics Collective at San Francisco State University (SFSU) with the expertise of blind access professionals. 

Emily Beitiks was the accessibility lead for the content creation of the exhibit. She is the co-director for the San Francisco Disability Cultural Center (the first civically funded disability culture center on the planet!), and prior to that, the director of the Longmore Institute on Disability. 

Nick Sousanis (SFSU), the lead creative organizer of the exhibit, is a Detroit native and was the first person to draw his dissertation in comics format, subsequently published as the graphic novel Unflattening.

View the exhibit anytime the Hatcher Library is open, and join us for an opening presentation on Friday, October 2nd, 1:00pm - 4:00pm.

combined_title: Lila Kadaj Exhibition: Tic Tic
description:
Lila Kadaj received her MFA from Wayne State University. Her work has been shown at numerous institutions, including the Detroit Institute of Arts, the Cranbrook Art Museum, and the Arab American National Museum.  She spent nearly 27 years teaching art at Detroit Public schools.

Artist statement: “When looking at a beautiful flower.  It’s just itself.  Just there......no .....it does not proclaim its purpose for blooming is to make people happy. It just is. Like standing in front of an easel and painting........just is.......no matter......what proclamations may be concluded to sway the viewer. Same thing goes for fine art.  It’s not about I am a woman....it’s not about I am a first generation Arab American.....it’s not about being a child of trauma....it’s not about a member of my family being gunned down on the street....it’s about being born a painter.....standing in front of my easel and working to create a "Piece of Fine Art". Not standing on some soap box and expecting my words to somehow qualify my painting. It’s the painting, drawing or sculpture that must speak on its own.......on how the artist......via the intellect and muse uses the elements to create something distinct and first rate.   It can be quiet or loud. I see so much very weak work uplifted not for its quality but because it’s in fashion.”

event_title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
combined_title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
description:
Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union.

Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky  portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration.  

“For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.”
— Galina Lembersky, daughter

Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director.

Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky.

combined_title: Black Birth Joy: Announcing Lane Hall’s Fall Exhibition
description:
Black Birth Joy by Tiana Lashae documents birth as a deeply personal story of connection, courage, tenderness, and joy. The photographs and stories in the exhibit challenge mainstream narratives that reduce Black birth to statistics and only amplify Black pregnant women's anxiety and hesitancy about navigating the maternal health care system. Instead, the exhibit offers evidence of joy, reminders of possibility, and a visual legacy for generations to come. 
 
Black Birth Joy was born from Lashae's belief that more positive birth stories of BIPOC families need to be seen and heard, and her photographs invite viewers to witness the people behind them: the mothers, babies, partners, families, and birthworkers. They create space for BIPOC families to see themselves represented with dignity and to witness the full range of birth experiences. Lashae's photographs also create a tangible record that can support conversations around quality of medical care, respectful treatment, and patient rights. The exhibit empowers women to prioritize and advocate for their birth experiences while also encouraging perinatal health professionals and birthworkers to center the humanity, dignity, and individual experiences of patients and families. 

The exhibit comprises over 30 photographs as well as stories of mothers whose births were documented by Lashae, a doula and birth/newborn photographer whose work has been published in Everyday Birth Magazine, an international publication. The physical exhibit is accompanied by a virtual component that encourages audiences to engage with each mother's birth story.

The Lane Hall Exhibit Space is sponsored by the Institute for Research on Women and Gender (IRWG) and the Department of Women’s and Gender Studies (WGS) at the University of Michigan.

combined_title: IPAH at 25: New Directions in the Study of Ancient History
event_subtitle: New Directions in the Study of Ancient History
description:
Join us for a one-day conference marking the twenty-fifth anniversary of the University of Michigan’s Interdepartmental Program in Ancient History.

The conference will bring together invited speakers from the University of Michigan alumni community and institutions across North America and Europe to reflect on major transformations in the study of ancient history over the past several decades. Speakers will consider the evolution of their own scholarship and the broader disciplinary shifts that have shaped graduate training, research methods, and the expanding horizons of the field.

MORNING SESSION
Redefining Ancient History: Boundaries, Connections, and Scales
 
9:00-9:30 AM: Brendan Haug
“Introductory Remarks: Is there a Science of Ancient History?”
 
9:30-10:15 AM: Nathanael Andrade
“From ‘Greek and Roman’ to ‘Ancient’: Implications of the Shift”
The transformation of the Interdepartmental Program for Greek and Roman History (IPGRH) into the Interdepartmental Program for Ancient History (IPAH) reflects broader changes in how ancient historians conceptualize both their subjects and their discipline. Drawing on my own research, this paper explores the shifts in approaches to ancient peoples as subjects of empires, members of confessional communities, and participants in a connected Afro-Eurasian world, while considering questions of who has the authority to study and claim their pasts.
 
10:15-11:00 AM: Denise Demetriou
“A Connected Ancient Mediterranean World: The Challenges and Rewards of Bridging Disciplinary Divides”
Adopting a Mediterranean perspective and bridging the traditional disciplinary divide between Classics and Ancient Near Eastern studies can illuminate neglected dimensions of ancient history, including patterns of population and cultural interaction. This paper reflects on the challenges and rewards of such interdisciplinary approaches and considers their implications for the future direction of the field.
 
11:00-11:45 AM: Jenn Finn
“All (Royal) Roads Start in Ann Arbor: The Grammar of Imperial Legitimacy between Classics and Cuneiform Studies”
Across four millennia, rulers from the ancient Near East to Rome appropriated the cultural heritage and monumental landscapes of the past to construct imagined boundaries of imperial authority. Drawing on research that bridges Classics and Assyriology, this paper examines such practices as a form of soft power fundamental to imperial strategy and legitimacy.
 
11:45 AM-12:30 PM: Peter Bang
“Matching the Global with the Local: Ancient History between Macro and Micro”
 
 
AFTERNOON SESSION
Writing Ancient Histories: Narratives, Experiences, and Contemporary Relevance
 
2:00-2:45 PM: Cam Grey
“Social Historians Telling Stories”
How do social historians reconcile the particularity of individual anecdotes with the ambitions of grand historical narratives? This paper reflects on the tensions and occasional convergences between these modes of storytelling and considers the kinds of histories we can, could, and should construct from disparate forms of evidence.
 
2:45-3:30 PM: Emily Lamond
“The Ancient Body in Question”
Recent scholarship has increasingly approached disability in antiquity not simply as a medical condition but as a culturally constructed category shaped by social expectations and individual circumstances. Moving beyond familiar representations of Roman society as uniformly hostile to disabled bodies, this paper explores how disability could shape different dimensions of everyday experience and invites historians to reconstruct ancient individuals' relationships with their bodies in richer, more contextually sensitive ways.
 
3:30-4:15 PM: Adriaan Lanni
“Interdisciplinary Approaches to Ancient Law at UM and Beyond: Juries as a Check on Politicized Prosecutions in Athens and Today”
Building on Michigan’s longstanding tradition of interdisciplinary legal history, this paper explores how comparisons between ancient and modern legal systems can illuminate both Athenian law and contemporary legal problems. Focusing on politically motivated prosecutions in classical Athens, it argues that Athenian juries exercised a form of prosecutorial discretion rather than simply engaging in jury nullification, and considers what this comparison might teach us about the potential of modern juries to check politically motivated prosecutions.
 
4:15-5:00 PM: Katherine Blouin
“The Moral of the Story: On Doing Ancient History in Times of Collapse”

combined_title: Like the flowing river: An exhibition by Tomoyuki Ueno
description:
Artist Tomoyuki Ueno creates individual works and installations where nature appears to be in an endless conversation with form, one echoing the other, a repetition. They are a combination of certainty and ephemerality, as if hinged between living and loss. The specificity of Ueno’s sculptural works reads like poetry. Ueno’s installation offers visitors time away, for contemplation, to draw inward, to come inside, to ask the question, “How are art and the everyday intertwined?” Honoring the Buddhist philosophy of impermanence, one becomes a continuation of the other. The artist intends the space to offer a restorative and meditative experience.

This exhibition includes artworks created from natural materials foraged by the artist while in artist residency in Ann Arbor.

*The title refers to the opening line of Hōjōki, written by 13th-century Japanese Buddhist monk Kamo no Chōmei: "The flow of the river is ceaseless, and the water is never the same…"*

Prints & Book Objects from Detroit 2020–2026

October 27 - November 19 
Public Reception: Friday, November 13 from 4:30-6pm.

Small Works was a print shop ran by Li Chen & Gerald Schulze, in Detroit, MI, from 2020–2026. Mariana Matos joined as the studio assistant, and later studio manager, in 2024. Over those six years, the business grew from an extension of their design practice to a community space that hosts more than 70 classes a year, open studio for the public, and year long funded fellowships that investigate practice in art and design related to the Book Arts. In 2026, they decided to expand community programming, and to accommodate this expansion closed Small Works, and formed Center for the Book Arts Detroit (BAD) which operates in the same space.

This exhibition is a eulogy for the former Small Works shop, and a celebration of all the people who made work here. It also serves to show what is possible as a community, when they share space and create work together. 

The work featured is a collection of things printed by Small Works, by their studiomates Diskette Press, the publisher Maamoul Press, and by the community that uses the space.

event_title: Beyond who knows whom: Three-way social network analysis
combined_title: Beyond who knows whom: Three-way social network analysis: Nynke Niezink
description: Network data involving three roles (e.g., sender, receiver, and target or perceiver) can be represented as a three-dimensional array. Such three-way networks arise naturally in social science research, but their analysis poses challenges. Although substantive questions often involve social mechanisms driving network change, no longitudinal methods for three-way networks currently exist. Moreover, data collection on three-way networks places a heavy burden on respondents, so sometimes only partial information is available. This talk presents two methodological contributions that start to address these limitations: a longitudinal model for fully observed three-way network data, and an inferential framework that uses two-way network data to learn about three-way relations. I will illustrate through applications what new empirical questions these methods enable us to address.

description:
Zell Visiting Writers Series craft lecutures are free and open to the public and will be offered both virtually (via Zoom) and in person (Michigan League, Henderson Room 3rd floor). Seats are offered on a first come, first served basis; please arrive early to secure a spot. Login here (no pre-registration needed): https://myumi.ch/ZellWriters26

Tony Tulathimutte is the author of *Private Citizens* and* Rejection*. A graduate of Stanford University's Symbolic Systems program, he took creative writing classes with Adam Johnson, ZZ Packer, and Elizabeth Tallent. After graduating, he published a handful of stories, one of which won an O. Henry Award, as he worked for a small Bay Area UX firm. He got accepted to the Iowa Writers' Workshop the same week he was laid off in 2010.

At Iowa he finished most of a draft of his debut novel *Private Citizens*, which was called "the first great Millennial novel" by *New York Magazine* after its publication in 2016, and received a Whiting Writers' Award. In 2017 he founded CRIT, an independent class he teaches out of his apartment in Brooklyn, whose alumni have gone on to publish 34 books to date. He has written for *The Paris Review, N+1, The New York Times, The New Republic, The Believer, Playboy,* The Nation, and others.

Tony's second book is a novel-in-stories, *Rejection*, published in 2024. *Rejection* has been translated into seven languages, and was nominated for the National Book Award, the Story Prize, and the Clark Prize, and received a Jack Galef Literary Arts award. He is currently a Visiting Professor at the Iowa Writers' Workshop.

description:
Join us at Matthaei Botanical Gardens for an art exhibit by Justin Johnson Nodagwzëwêk gi gdankobthëgnenanêk (our ancestors are heard): Contemporary Visions in Native American Art.  September 29 - November 15, 2026.

Artist Bio

“Bozho, Justin Johnson nde zhnëkas, Eau Claire ndë wtthbya. Mshiké ndodem minė Bodéwadmi ndaw.” (“Hello, my name is Justin Johnson, I come from Eau Claire. My clan is turtle and I am Potawatomi”). 

My name is Justin Johnson, Native name Thitthishkewé. I’m a visual artist whose work is deeply shaped by my Potawatomi heritage. Raised in Coloma, Michigan, my artistic path began in childhood and continued through grade school and high school, eventually leading to me studying at Kendall College of Art & Design for four years. My art is a reflection of both personal expression and cultural tradition, honoring the interconnectedness of people, animals, land, and spirit. Guided by intuition, ancestral knowledge, and the natural world. I’m always seeking new ways to tell stories through my work. My drawings are inspiration from tribal stories, culture, and values that have been passed down through generations. I have collaborated with the Pokagon Band on numerous projects, including traditional storybooks and illustrations. Aswell as permanent collections at the Pokagon Band Administration Building and the Pokagon Health Services building, and artwork featured in the Four Winds Casino gift shop. Some other projects and exhibtions that I’ve participated in would be the Native American exhibition at the Krasl Art Center and a featured as the cover artist with a six-page article in PAN-O-PLY magazine. My murals can be found at the Grand Rapids Public Museum, the Edwardsburg (Cass County District) Library, and the Buchanan District Library. Currently, I’m collaborating with Northwestern University on a new mural for their football stadium. Through diverse body of work, my work continues to share the stories, values, and traditions of his heritage with a wide audience.

Artist Statement

My work is deeply rooted in my culture, which shapes both my perspective and my creative process. We see ourselves as part of the Earth, not separate from it—every act, every gesture, is an exchange. When we take, we give. This relationship is woven into the art I make, which follows the tradition known as Woodlands Style, or Legendary Style. It’s not the invention of any one person. It has been handed down, shaped by countless hands and stories over generations. This style is often described as “x-ray” painting. With vivid colors and layered lines, I try to reveal the inner spirit of animals, plants, and people—sometimes physical, sometimes spiritual. There’s a rhythm to it that still echoes the Great Lakes region: bold, luminous, and full of life. Each piece is a story that’s been told and retold, woven across time, just like the spirits that guide us. As an artist, I try to reflect these values in everything I do. Even when we drift from the old ways, our spirit keeps us connected. My work is a reminder—a visual invitation to reconnect, to live more intentionally, and to honor the balance and respect that our traditions teach.

event_title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism
combined_title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism: Nicola Barham, Curator
description:
The lifelike naturalistic bodies of Greek and Roman sculpture have been a source of wonder since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Italian Renaissance artist Vasari identified the ancient world as the time “when sculpture rose to its greatest height.” But close likenesses of the natural world are not the only visual products of the ancient past. This exhibition traces alternative visual trends in the ancient Roman world that today would be considered examples of abstraction. It focuses on monuments and motifs long pushed to the margins of our accounts of ancient art. Oversize arrangements of interlocking shapes pulsate in bold block colors from tombs, temples, and homes; stylized animals flicker into view, only to collapse once more into bright geometric arrangements; and artists adopt experimental shorthands for the depiction of space across media. Anticipating recent interests in color and form, the visual trends of antiquity emerge as far more varied than has long been told.

*Ancient Abstractions is on view from November 5, 2026, through February 28, 2027, during regular museum hours (Tuesday–Friday, 10:00 AM–4:00 PM, and Saturday–Sunday, 11:00 AM–4:00 PM; closed Mondays and university holidays.*

description:
From September 2025 through December 2026, Stamps Gallery is partnering in a curatorial collaboration with two Southeast Michigan-based, artist-run project spaces led by Stamps alumni: C.Y.N.K. Studios, directed by Sally Clegg (Lecturer III and Student Exhibition Coordinator, MFA ’20) and Abhishek Narula (MFA ’20); and Sometimes Space, directed by Nathan Byrne (Lecturer I, MFA ’21). Each space hosts dozens of artists annually for exhibitions, performances, and events, fostering experimental work and building community. For this project, Byrne, Clegg, and Narula have been commissioned to reimagine the pillars on Division Street that flank the gallery. In response, they’ve curated six artists to create new work for the pillars over three cycles:

Phase 1 (September 12 - December 12) artists: Amelia Burns (Cranbrook MFA ’23) and Erin McKenna (MFA ’20)
Phase 2 (January 12 - August 12) artists: Sally Clegg (MFA ’20) and Kim Karlsrud (MFA ’20)
Phase 3 (September 11 - December 11) artists: Abhishek Narula (MFA ’20) and Nathan Byrne (MFA ’21)
Phase 3 

Curated by Sometimes Space: Abhishek Narula (entry pillar)
Curated by CYNK Studios: Nathan Byrne (courtyard pillar)

Artist Statements/Bios

Abhishek Narula, Compressions 
Compressions is an installation comprised of 416 industrial-grade zip ties, cinched around the entry pillar of the Stamps Gallery. The pillar measures roughly 110 inches in circumference, requiring two ties per row to wrap around it, resulting in 208 rows. The humble zip tie, typically used to hang and bind other material, is relegated to its functional properties rendering it unprepossessing and easily dismissed. The zip tie in this installation, instead serves as an object of aesthetic possibility, pulling it out of its usual background role to become the work itself. The resulting composition is a proposal to dwell, to slow down, and to simply see the pillar.

Abhishek Narula is an artist, designer, and educator who works across sculpture, installation, sound, and video. His practice takes the form of interventions, working with what is already present. He reorients and disrupts objects and sites in order to open up formal possibilities and poetic experiences within the familiar. He is influenced by physical and digital infrastructural systems that sustain modern life and culture. His work treats this ambience itself as raw material for aesthetic inquiry, exploring themes of labor, precarity, temporality and the sublime. Narula earned his MFA in Studio Art from the University of Michigan Stamps School of Art & Design and his MS/BS in Electrical Engineering from the Georgia Institute of Technology. His work has been exhibited at national and international venues such as the Ammerman Center for Arts and Technology, Science Gallery Detroit, Speculum Artium Media Festival in Slovenia, New Media Caucus (NMC), WaveFarm, The Boulder Public Library, The Hyde Park Art Center, Sector 2337 Art Gallery & Printing Press, Tangible Embedded Interaction (TEI), International Symposium of Electronic Arts (ISEA), among others. He is a Robotics Systems Designer and Lecturer in the Robotics Department at the University of Michigan. Website / Instagram

Nathan Byrne, Equally To Be Loved
Equally To Be Loved is an image / object scaled to and installed upon the courtyard pillar of Stamps Gallery. The image is of a spontaneous sculpture made in 2017 during the first day of an artist residency at the Recology San Francisco A.I.R. Program. The sculpture was constructed in a storage container studio using 14 discrete objects that were in his studio upon entry. For Byrne, this work embodies the energy and spirit of a studio at the start of a particularly fecund period of making. This work speaks to the artist’s interest in embodied experience of space, archival and site responsiveness, as well as his ongoing engagement with found materials. Byrne considers this project to be a far-flung sequel to his MFA thesis exhibition Equally Empty, which was shown at Stamps Gallery in 2021. Equally To Be Loved is the second line of the Buddhist mantra from which both titles are derived.

Nathan Byrne is an artist / educator / curator currently based in Detroit, MI. Through spatial and archive responsive projects, he reimagines, and explores within frameworks such as language, the passage of time, and contemplation. Intrigued by the potential of conveying phenomenal, transformative, and emotive states through materiality, process, and placement, he negotiates the pliability of the viewer’s encounters with objects and environments. Byrne holds an MFA in Art from the University of Michigan Stamps School of Art & Design and a BA in Studio Art and Art History from San Francisco State University. He has been a Lecturer at Stamps School of Art & Design since the Fall of 2022. His work is exhibited widely nationally and he is a recipient of the VSC Fellowship at Vermont Studio Center. He has been awarded numerous artist residencies including Anderson Ranch Arts Center, I-Park, KHN Center for the Arts, Prairie Ronde, Recology San Francisco A.I.R. Program, and Rockland Woods. combined_title: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”
description:
Changes over the course of the nineteenth century in how Americans voted, from voice vote to public ballot box to private voting booth, also saw changes in the material culture that surrounded voting. Ballots and ballot boxes, campaign pins and ribbons, blank lists and pre-printed party tickets, lanterns and banners–the creative forces of the American print industry filled the country’s cities and small towns with the ephemera of electioneering.

As you look at the items in this exhibit, think about what they tell us about how Americans in the past felt about voting, and about how voting felt. How did Election Days feel when they were full of parades and music and public drinking? What was it like to vote when everyone around you knew who you voted for? And, most of all, who counted as a voter, and who did the counting?

On view September 11-December 22, weekdays from 12-4 pm.

event_title: A Hole Lot of Uncertainty: Probabilistic Evaluation of Archaeological Subsurface Survey

event_subtitle: Dr. William Pestle,  Director of Education, U-M Kelsey Museum of Archaeology
description: In regions with low surface visibility, archaeologists often turn to systematic subsurface testing for purposes of site location. While numerous factors impact both the effectiveness and efficiency of these prospection efforts, “cookie-cutter” survey strategies are often employed without a thorough examination of their costs and benefits, and the results of such surveys are subject to erroneous interpretation when factors like effectiveness and limits of detection are not taken into account. In this presentation, we examine how a simulation-based approach that incorporates prior data can probabilistically determine the effectiveness and efficiency of different survey strategies. Beyond permitting the design of survey strategies that maximize the possibility of site detection and husband precious resources (time, money), this method also permits the generation of post hoc correction factors that make possible the critical evaluation and direct comparison of previous survey results.

description:
Curated by Srimoyee Mitra

Stamps Gallery kicks off the fall 2026 semester with an ambitious mid-career survey of interdisciplinary artist Cosmo Whyte. Born and raised in Jamaica, Whyte completed a BFA from Bennington College and earned an MFA from the University of Michigan. He is currently a faculty member at the School of the Arts and Architecture, UCLA.

This exhibition brings together two central concerns that animate Whyte’s artistic practice: the archive, both personal and public, as a site of disturbance; and migration as a lived experience of refuge, refusal, and reinvention. In Whyte’s work, the archive is never static or neutral. Rather, it is a contested space where official histories encounter memory, inheritance, and the fragments of stories carried across generations. His practice moves within this charged interstitial terrain, between what has been recorded and what has been remembered, between institutional knowledge and embodied experience. Whyte invites the viewer to consider the fluidity of geographic borders and layered cultural identities that have persisted despite societal unrest caused by racial and socio-economic hierarchies across generations. In an era of intensified border politics and renewed debates over national identity, Whyte’s work offers a timely meditation on memory, movement, and belonging.

event_title: EIHS Workshop: Childhood, Gendered Affinities, and Structures of Power
combined_title: EIHS Workshop: Childhood, Gendered Affinities, and Structures of Power: Rachael Barrett, Ayriel Marie Coleman, Robert Diaz, and Henry E. Chen, LaKisha Michelle Simmons, moderator
event_subtitle: Rachael Barrett, Ayriel Marie Coleman, Robert Diaz, and Henry E. Chen, LaKisha Michelle Simmons, moderator
description:
**Note: The location of this workshop has changed to the Michigan Room in the Michigan League.

In the face of global democratic backsliding, feminist demands have gained renewed visibility even as patriarchal, racial, and class-based violence and exclusion have become increasingly normalized across regional, national, and local boundaries. In this context, childhood, and girlhood in particular, has emerged as a matter of political, moral, and ideological contestation. Situating these contemporary struggles within a broader historical perspective, however, reveals that gendered childhood, as a concept and social project, has long served as a site onto which collective fears, social aspirations, and competing visions of citizenship and belonging are projected. Indeed, Marcia Chatelain's work has shown that, during the Great Migration, Black girlhood in Chicago’s South Side represented a potential path to social mobility, even as it was undermined by indiscriminate lynchings, labor demands in an expanding commercial market, a punitive judicial system, and sexual victimization. This scholarship raises important historical and methodological questions, such as: Who is afforded the innocence and vulnerability of childhood? In what ways have race, gender, and class together impacted public discourses regarding what it means to be a “good citizen”? How have crises around racialized, gendered, and classed identity inspired unexpected historical affinities and collaborations? How might historians navigate (and overcome) gaps and silences in the traditional archive, which have effectively erased the perspectives of racialized and working-class children?

This event presented by the Eisenberg Institute for Historical Studies. It is made possible in part by a generous contribution from Kenneth and Frances Aftel Eisenberg.

description:
Kathleen Beck performs on the Charles Baird Carillon, an instrument of 53 bronze bells located inside the Burton Memorial Tower. The largest bell, which strikes the hour, weighs 12 tons, while the smallest bell, 4½ octaves above, weighs just 15 pounds.

Thirty-minute recitals are performed on the Charles Baird Carillon at noon every weekday that classes are in session, followed by visitor Q&A with the carillonist. The bell chamber may be accessed via a combination of elevator and stairs. Take the elevator to the highest floor possible (floor 8), and then climb two flights of stairs (39 steps) to the bell chamber (floor 10). Hearing protection earmuffs are provided for visitors. event_title: Who Gets Connected? Network Drivers of Racial Inequality in Tie Formation at Work
combined_title: Who Gets Connected? Network Drivers of Racial Inequality in Tie Formation at Work: Mabel Abraham, Columbia Business School
description: Intraorganizational networks are critical for careers, yet Black employees derive fewer benefits from networks than their White counterparts, partly because they form fewer cross-race instrumental ties. Extant research has attributed these disparities to interpersonal mechanisms whereby dissimilar individuals are less likely to connect. This paper moves beyond dyadic explanations by theorizing how triadic closure—whereby shared contacts increase the likelihood of tie formation—varies by race. We argue that the presence of shared contacts creates the opportunity structure for racial disparities in ties formed by reducing transparency and diffusing accountability, particularly when those ties provide access to career-advancing work. Using a longitudinal network dataset combining personnel and staffing records of 2,481 new hires in a professional services firm, we estimate the causal effect of having shared contacts on subsequent year-end tie formation. We find that the effect of shared contacts on subsequent tie formation is approximately 94% lower for Black than for White new hires, although no such gap exists when ties form in the absence of shared contacts. These findings advance our understanding of the network drivers of racial disparities, demonstrate that triadic closure is socially differentiated, and show how networks generate unequal access to career-advancing opportunities.

event_title: Confidence, Inattention and First-Moment Effects of Information (joint with Ben Golub, Northwestern University)
combined_title: Confidence, Inattention and First-Moment Effects of Information (joint with Ben Golub, Northwestern University): Stephen Morris, Massachusetts Institute of Technology
event_subtitle: Stephen Morris, Massachusetts Institute of Technology
description: We study canonical coordination models – with linear best responses to an uncertain state and to others' average action - in which, under a common prior, information has only second-moment effects. With heterogeneous priors and asymmetric information, expected behavior itself depends on the information structure, and we characterize how. As coordination strengthens, behavior converges to a focal mean of groups' prior means, weighted by size and resoluteness, the share of the prior retained in the posterior: the consensus overweights confident and inattentive groups. In a team production problem inducing these best responses, welfare depends primarily on the focal mean, which agents unanimously prefer to increase: everyone would prefer that more optimistic agents be less precisely informed, and so more resolute. When signals are noisy readings of a public announcement, varying the announcement's clarity reallocates influence over the focal mean.  When coordination is mediated by a network, network positions and resoluteness effects interact in a way that is qualitatively richer than in a homogeneous population.

combined_title: AIM Seminar: Geometry for Physics Simulation: Oliver Gross (Computer Science and Engineering, University of California San Diego)
event_subtitle: Oliver Gross (Computer Science and Engineering, University of California San Diego)
description:
Abstract: Advances in simulation and scientific machine learning have made computation an engine of discovery. For increasingly complex physical systems, however, computational scale and model expressiveness alone may not suffice for faithful simulation, exploration, and inverse design. General-purpose representations often describe a space much larger than the set of physically admissible states. Computing in this larger space can require substantial effort to ensure that solutions respect the underlying geometry, topology, and conservation laws. A complementary path is to make this structure explicit. Through examples ranging from bending rods and slithering snakes to fluid flows and magnetic fields in plasmas, this talk shows how geometric insight can make difficult problems computationally tractable, how the resulting structure can be preserved and encoded in algorithms, and how the exchange among theory, discretization, and application yields new mathematics alongside more effective computational tools.

combined_title: Alan J. Hunt Memorial Lecture-U-M Biomedical Engineering: "Physical principles of cardiac sarcomere organization in health and disease," featuring Alex Dunn, Ph.D.
event_subtitle: "Physical principles of cardiac sarcomere organization in health and disease," featuring Alex Dunn, Ph.D.
description:
2026 Alan J. Hunt Memorial Lecture

Physical principles of cardiac sarcomere organization in health and disease

Abstract:
The remarkable capabilities of living tissues reflect the self-assembly of biological macromolecules into structures far larger and more complex than their individual components. The Dunn laboratory seeks to understand the physical principles that allow molecular interactions to produce organized, functional tissues. In this talk, I will focus on cardiomyocytes, whose contractile machinery provides a striking example of biological self-assembly. Using single-molecule force spectroscopy, we find that α-actinin-2, a core component of the sarcomeric Z-disc, binds actin in a strongly force- and direction-dependent manner. This behavior suggests a mechanism by which forces generated during contraction can help organize and stabilize sarcomeric architecture. In parallel, we are investigating how inherited cardiomyopathy mutations perturb sarcomere mechanics and organization. Genetically encoded force sensors reveal how disease-associated myosin mutations alter force propagation within sarcomeres, while cryo-electron tomography shows how these mutations disrupt sarcomere order at the molecular scale. These and other data suggest that alterations in sarcomeric organization may be intimately linked to the development of cardiomyopathy. Finally, I will describe emerging approaches for scaling single-molecule biophysics from measurements of individual interactions to systematic surveys of hundreds of molecular variants. These approaches open the door to studies of mechanobiology at scale and to the design and characterization of new molecular mechanosensors.

Bio:
Alex Dunn is a Professor in the Department of Chemical Engineering at Stanford University. His research focuses on understanding how living cells sense mechanical stimuli, with particular interests in stem cell biology and tissue engineering. Dr. Dunn worked as a postdoctoral scholar with James Spudich in the Department of Biochemistry at the Stanford University School of Medicine. He received his Ph.D. at the California Institute of Technology under the direction of Harry Gray, where his work focused on understanding the catalytic mechanism selective C-H bond oxidation by cytochrome P450 enzymes. His work has been recognized with numerous awards, including the Hertz Fellowship, the Burroughs Wellcome Career Award at the Scientific Interface, the NIH Director’s New Innovator Award, and the HHMI Faculty Scholar Award.

event_title: HET Seminar | Euclidean Wormholes and Axion Cosmology
combined_title: HET Seminar | Euclidean Wormholes and Axion Cosmology: Gary Shiu (Wisconsin)
description: Axions arise ubiquitously in theories of particle physics and quantum gravity and may play important roles in cosmology, from inflation and dark matter to dark energy. This raises a basic question: does quantum gravity constrain the allowed parameter space of axions, and can such constraints have observable consequences? I will discuss how Euclidean wormholes provide a surprising connection between these questions and quantum gravity. I will first review the axionic Weak Gravity Conjecture (aWGC), including the importance of its order-one coefficient for axion phenomenology, and then describe how Euclidean wormholes may give rise to this bound. I will discuss the perturbative stability of axion wormholes and their explicit realization in string theory, both in flat space and in AdS. Finally, I will present recent work showing that the aWGC can arise directly from the nonperturbative fragmentation of Euclidean wormholes into charged defects. Requiring such fragmentation to lower the Euclidean action fixes the action-to-charge bound and its order-one coefficient, and reveals a direct connection to the Imaginary Distance Bound. This suggests that quantum-gravitational constraints on axions can be understood as conditions on the non-perturbative stability of gravitational saddles, with implications for axion cosmology and the consistency of effective field theories.

event_title: On the Algebra of Moving Window Calculations
combined_title: On the Algebra of Moving Window Calculations: Daniel Rockmore (Dartmouth)
description: Moving window calculations arise throughout applied mathematics, computer science, and engineering. Familiar examples include moving sums, maxima, and filters, but the same basic problem also appears in more general windowed recurrences. In this talk, we show that a large class of such calculations admits a common algebraic formulation. In the associative setting, moving window calculations can be recast as exponentiation in a semidirect product, bringing efficient powering algorithms to bear. In more general settings, semi-associativity provides the right framework for representing compositions of updates and understanding when efficient computation is still possible. This point of view not only unifies a broad family of examples, but also leads naturally to compact vectorized implementations, making the methods well suited to modern GPU architectures. This is joint work with David Maslen.

event_title: Student Algebraic Geometry: Compactifications of Siegel Modular Varieties
combined_title: Student Algebraic Geometry: Compactifications of Siegel Modular Varieties: Jacob Zweifler
description: The Siegel upper half-space H_g serves as a natural generalization of the upper half-plane. Indeed, just as M_{1,1} = A_1 is the quotient H/SL_2(Z), one can show that A_g, the space of principally polarized abelian varieties of dimension g, is isomorphic to H_g/Sp_{2g}(Z). More generally, one can consider spaces H_g/Gamma for any arithmetic subgroup Gamma in Sp_{2g}(Q). Unlike M_g, which admits the canonical Deligne-Mumford compactification, these spaces admit many natural compactifications with different geometric properties. In this talk, we introduce H_g/Gamma, the Siegel modular varieties, and discuss various compactifications such as the Baily–Borel compactification and toroidal compactifications. We then focus on the specific case of g = 2 to showcase the beautiful arithmetic that occurs even in this small case.

event_subtitle: Adrienne Tsikewa, University of California, Riverside
description:
Join us for a colloquium presented by Adrienne Tsikewa (University of California Riverside) in North Quad 2435 on Friday, November 13, 2026, from 4-5:30 PM!

Title: “It could be a stepping stone”: Zunglish and language ideologies

Abstract: Language mixing is a prevailing linguistic practice under conditions of language contact that has been extensively analyzed and theorized by linguists (e.g. Muysken 2000, Bullock & Toribio 2009, Hickey 2010). When one of the languages in contact is English, language mixing results in a variety that “liberally blends elements from English and from one or more local languages” (Schneider 2016: 341). These hybrid English varieties are a global phenomenon and are often referred to by lexical blends that combine English and the local language or community name (e.g. Spanglish, Chinglish, Singlish). Due to the stigma frequently associated with hybrid English (Lambert 2018, Schneider 2016), connotations associated with these terms are predominantly negative, aligning with prevalent language purism ideologies or deficit-based language ideologies of language mixing as poor or broken English. Awareness and understanding of such language ideologies is critical to Native American language contexts, as without this knowledge “scholars and researchers-both Native and non-Native-cannot hope to understand Native American languages and the ways speakers use them, change them, and renew them.”(Kroskrity & Field 2009:10)

In this talk, I present one part of my larger dissertation study on bilingual language practices and ideologies in Zuni Pueblo, New Mexico. My analysis focuses on language ideologies towards Zunglish, or language mixing involving Zuni and English, expressed during interviews with adult participants of various ages and with various levels of ability in the Zuni language. I show that some of the participants express ideologies of deficiency and language purism toward Zunglish, while others view language mixing as a necessity and as a reflection of hon a:wan A:shiwi ‘our Zuni people’ living in two worlds. I conclude by reflecting on how these ideologies can hinder community members, in particular younger generations, from speaking Zuni and how valuing rather than disparaging bilingual practices is essential to creating the conditions for A:shiwi who wish to gain confidence in using the language.

References:

handbook of linguistic code-switching. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

Beliefs, practices and struggles in Indian Country. Tucson, AZ: University of Arizona
Press.

description:
The Department of Strings presents a guest artist master class with cellist Juliette Herlin (Texas Christian University School of Music). Free and open to the public.

ABOUT THE GUEST ARTIST

Celebrated for her poetic and deeply communicative playing, French cellist JULIETTE HERLIN has been recognized by *Strings* as a “rising star” and praised for her “impressive artistry” (*San Francisco Classical Voice*). She has performed across the U.S., Europe, Asia, and South America, appearing in prestigious venues including Alice Tully Hall in New York, the Kennedy Center in Washington, D.C., the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées and the Musée du Louvre in Paris, and the Zhuhai and Chongqing Grand Theaters in China.

Herlin’s debut album, *Dialogue: Debussy & Schumann*, recorded with pianist Kevin Ahfat and released in the summer of 2025 on Orchid Classics, reached the top of the classical charts with over 2.5 million streams. Hailed as an “impressive debut album” (*Strings*), it was awarded five stars from *Diapason* and featured in *The Strad* and *Gramophone* magazines.

2025–26 season highlights include a performance of Paquito D’Rivera’s Cello and Clarinet Concerto, *The Journey*, with the composer himself, Beethoven’s Triple Concerto with the Round Top Festival Orchestra, conducted by Carl St. Clair, and recitals across the U.S. Previous highlights include Herlin’s New York Concerto debut at Merkin Hall and the North American premiere of Camille Saint-Saëns’s Third Cello Sonata as part of a recital presented by the Music Academy of the West.

An avid chamber musician, she has performed with artists such as Gérard Caussé, Martin Chalifour, Glenn Dicterow, Alex Kerr, Teng Li, Richie Hawley, Anthony Marwood, Nicolas Namoradze, Roger Tapping, and Donald Weilerstein. Herlin is the cellist of the Aletheia Piano Trio, alongside pianist Fei-Fei and violinist Francesca dePasquale. Formed in 2013 at the Juilliard School, the trio made its debut at the Rose Studio and Alice Tully Hall at Lincoln Center in New York, and at the Terrace Theater at the Kennedy Center in Washington, D.C. They have since performed across the U.S., made their Korean debut with the Beethoven Triple Concerto alongside the Gustav Mahler Orchestra, and toured China in 2018 and 2019, performing in Poly Theaters throughout the country.

She has been invited to perform at prestigious series and festivals, including the Chamber Music Society of Palm Beach, Yellow Barn, Shenson Chamber Music Concerts, Shandelee Music Festival, Sundays Live at LACMA, Concerts in the Barn, the Chamber Music Society of Logan, Friends of Chamber Music Reading, Dame Myra Hess Memorial Concerts, the Festival International Violoncello León in Mexico, and the Festival Jeunes Talents in France. Her performances have been broadcast on *Performance Today*, BBC Radio 3, CBC, and major classical radio stations across the US and Europe. 

Winner of the Yamaha Music Foundation of Europe String Competition, Juliette is also the recipient of first prizes at the International Vatelot/Rampal Music Competition and the UFAM Competition in Paris, as well as a Beverly Hills National Auditions winner. She has been invited to be guest principal of the Dallas Chamber Symphony, Fort Worth Symphony, and Kaleidoscope Chamber Orchestra. Additionally, she has performed with the Los Angeles Philharmonic, the Paris Opera, and the Orchestre Philharmonique de Radio-France.

As a dedicated advocate for contemporary music, Herlin has worked closely with prominent composers such as Kaija Saariaho and Jörg Widmann, and premiered many new works. Eager to discover various repertoires and explore historically informed performance, she has collaborated with jazz legend Wayne Shorter and bassist Esperanza Spalding, clarinetist Paquito D’Rivera, as well as studied baroque cello with Bruno Cocset and Phoebe Carrai.

Herlin is Assistant Professor of Cello at TCU’s School of Music and the co-founder/director of the Texas Chamber Music Institute. Additionally, she has been invited to present masterclasses at institutions such as the Manhattan School of Music, Oberlin Conservatory, and the San Francisco Conservatory of Music, and in China, Colombia, Mexico, and Denmark. In the summer, she is on faculty at the Round Top Festival and the International Cello Institute. Admitted at the age of sixteen to the Conservatoire National Supérieur de Musique de Paris (CNSMDP), Herlin obtained her Bachelor and Master of Music degrees studying with Jérôme Pernoo. She pursued her studies at the Juilliard School with Richard Aaron and received her Doctor of Musical Arts degree from the University of Southern California under the guidance of Ralph Kirshbaum. She plays an anonymous italian cello (c. 1830 from Perugia) and is honored to be a Bärenreiter Ambassador.

description: Engendering Respectful Communities (ERC) is a one session workshop that engages graduate students in meaningful dialogue about various forms of sexual misconduct they may encounter in both professional and social spaces, and provides resources for intervention or support in such circumstances.The primary goal of the workshop is to address complexities experienced by graduate students as they engage in bystander intervention, so that participants gain an increase in awareness of barriers to action and familiarity with strategic planning to overcome them. The workshop also introduces participants to on-campus resources and provides knowledge on how sexual misconduct can unfold in graduate-specific settings.The ERC workshop uses small-group circles intended to promote active reflection and space to build community. The procedure of circles is introduced at the beginning of the workshop in order to help participants get used to the process, which they do through a circle for introductions and value-sharing for the workshop space. These circles depict various, realistic scenarios related to sexual misconduct within the graduate community. The circle process allows circle members to process the monologues, reflect on complexities with identity and power dynamics within them, name potential barriers to intervention, and think of various ways in which they might respond if faced with similar situations. The circles provide a way to foster collective building of ideas, where participants learn from one another and all input is equally valued. Participants are encouraged to share but can always pass if desired, creating an environment where participation is open but not forced. Due to the participatory nature of the workshop, if you are to arrive more than 20 minutes late, we will ask you to re-register for another workshop session.If you have any questions about or concerns with taking this workshop, or are in need of an exemption, please contact jhippe@umich.edu or fill out this form. We know some students come to campus having already experienced harm. If you have circumstances that make completing this course challenging, please reach out to the GROWE team. SAPAC GROWE provides exemptions to the ERC workshop (where requirements are set in place) on a case by case basis. The Program Manager will communicate with students requesting exemptions via email and/or meet with students via zoom meetings to discuss their need for exemptions and provide any relevant and necessary resources.

combined_title: Mozart's Requiem and Brahms's Alto Rhapsody with Ann Arbor Symphony and UMS Choral Union
description:
While Mozart is not primarily known for sacred music, his final composition — the Requiem Mass — stands among his most sublime achievements.

Left unfinished at his death at age 35 and immortalized in the film Amadeus, the work was commissioned anonymously by a mysterious benefactor and was ultimately completed by Mozart’s student, Franz Xaver Süssmayr, from his sketches. As Mozart’s health declined, he is said to have believed he was composing the Requiem not for another, but for himself, a notion that deepens the work’s haunting resonance. Blending fear and hope with extraordinary emotional depth, the Requiem has captivated listeners for centuries.

This performance marks the UMS Choral Union’s first return to the piece in 80 years, in collaboration with the Ann Arbor Symphony Orchestra and its music director, Earl Lee. The program opens with Johannes Brahms’s rarely-performed Alto Rhapsody, a striking work for alto, male chorus, and orchestra.

PROGRAM
Johannes Brahms Alto Rhapsody, Op. 53
Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart Requiem in d minor, K. 626

Featuring:
Ann Arbor Symphony Orchestra
UMS Choral Union (
Scott Hanoian, UMS Choral Union music director)
Earl Lee, music director and conductor
Hera Hyesang Park, soprano

event_subtitle: American Mosaic: 250 Years — Music for Cello and Piano
description:
Duo Dolce presents an all-American program celebrating 250 years of American music, featuring works by composers including George Gershwin, Amy Beach, and Aaron Copland, alongside music shaped by immigrant and multicultural experiences. Together, these works create an American mosaic that reflects the country’s diverse cultural heritage, voices, and musical traditions.

PROGRAM

Antonín Dvorák: *Silent Woods op. 68 no. 5* (1891)
Aaron Copland: *Old American Songs* (1952) - *Simple Gifts*, *I Bought Me a Cat*, *At the River*
Harry Bulow: *Taegeuk* for solo cello (2024)
Allen McCullough: Trilogette for solo cello (2025) - *Homage - J.S.B.*, *Night Song*, *Perpetuum Mobile*
Erich Korngold: Romance Impromptu in E-flat major op. posth. (1946)
Chen-Yi: Romance of Hsiao and Ch’in (1995)
George Gershwin (arr. Ka-Wai Yu): Three Preludes (1926) - *Allegro ben ritmato e deciso*, *Andante con moto e poco rubato*, *Allegro ben ritmato e deciso*
William Grant Still: *Summerland* (1935)
Elliott Bark: *An-Nyoung: Goodbye/Hello* for cello and piano (2026) 
Amy Beach: Romance, Op.23 (1893)

ABOUT THE GUEST ARTISTS

KRISTEN YEON-JI YUN is a Clinical Professor in the Department of Music in the Patti and Rusty Rueff School of Design, Art, and Performance at Purdue University. She is an active soloist, chamber musician, scholar, and clinician. She has toured internationally, performing and giving master classes in countries including Malaysia, Mexico, Spain, France, Germany, and Taiwan. Her CD *Summerland* has received excellent reviews from *New Classics UK* and *American Record Guide* and was broadcast nationwide by major radio stations such as WQXR, WCNY, WBAA, and NPR’s *Sonatas and Soundscapes*. She earned her Doctor of Music degree in cello performance in 2012 from the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music, where she studied with the world-renowned cellist János Starker. Yun plays a 1766 Guersan cello.

PHOENIX PARK-KIM, Professor of Piano at Indiana Wesleyan University, has performed throughout the United States and internationally across Asia, Europe, and Latin America. A prizewinner in numerous competitions, she has appeared as a soloist with orchestras including the Korean Philharmonic and Atlantida Orchestra (Spain), performing concertos by Bach, Mozart, Beethoven, Chopin, Rachmaninoff, Hummel, and Florence Price. A passionate advocate for African-American composers, she has received a Lilly Research Grant and special congressional recognition. Dr. Park-Kim is a sought-after clinician and adjudicator whose students have earned regional and national honors, including MTNA National Competition finalist placements.

description:
Award-winning harmonies, wacky Western wit and high-yodeling adventures

40 years.  It seemed to go by in a blur, pounding the road, seeing the world, raising babies and sending them to college, mowing lawns, romances, marriages, high school drama, endless airports, the nights at the Hollywood Bowl, the night at the Red Barn in Louisville dodging various barroom projectiles, frozen diesel lines, blast furnace desert heat, hours of practice, late nights and early mornings, and lots and lots and lots of laughter.
 
40 years ago.  No laptops, no cellular phones, no Google, no downloads, no Skype, no Tweets, no Apple, no Microsoft, no texting, no electric cars, no Uber.  A different world.  But there were three young men with drive and wit who wanted to keep a special music alive.  They believed in preserving the heritage of Western Music and presenting it to a new generation.  They believed in entertaining, and they did so… entertaining themselves as well as the audience!  And they believed in creating original Western Music to continue the tradition, not just seal it in amber as a museum piece.  What they did not realize at the time was that they would be doing the same thing 40 years later.
 
40 years ago, Ranger Doug, Too Slim and the late Windy Bill Collins played that first date on the bitter cold evening of November 11th, 1977 at Herr Harry’s Frank N’ Stein Rathskeller in Nashville, and small listening room dates followed.  By August of the following year demand was building, and while Windy Bill left, Woody Paul joined, and the true professional beginnings of the band began at the Kentucky State Fair, where the trio played 10 days for $2500- and bought their own rooms and meals out of that!
 
A first wave followed, including appearances on Austin City Limits; recording contracts with Rounder, then MCA, then Columbia; guest appearances on the Grand Ole Opry leading to membership in 1982; and a three-year run on The Nashville Network with a TV show called “Tumbleweed Theater,” which yet in turn led to a seven-year run on public radio with “Riders Radio Theater.  People Magazine, interested in the Riders phenomenon, ran a story which happily caught the eye of a Hollywood producer.
 
And so the second wave broke, sending the boys to Hollywood to star in “Riders In The Sky” on CBS for a year on Saturday mornings, introducing them to yet another generation.  More recordings, endless show dates, and television appearances followed for a decade before the fine folks at Pixar called and asked the quartet – by this time they had been joined by Joey the Cowpolka King – to sing a tune called “Woody’s Roundup” in the movie “Toy Story 2.”  Thus, the third wave began, highlighted by a number of projects for Disney, including two albums, both of which won GRAMMY Awards!
 
The creation of satellite radio has recently given them a new platform, as they continue to produce episodes of the award winning “Classic Cowboy Corral” on Sirius/XM.
 
Still more road dates and recordings (several on their own Riders Radio Records label) and other film and television projects have filled the days and weeks and years, and since the quartet has slowed up very little, the numbers begin to add up:  an astonishing 7,200+ appearances, 35 years on the Grand Ole Opry, 40 records albums (well, now CDs,) and tours of all 50 states and all over the world.  Honors accumulated as well.  In addition to the two Grammy Awards, Riders received numerous awards from the Western Music Association, including the highest: membership in the Western Music Hall of Fame; numerous Wrangler awards from the Cowboy Hall of Fame and Western Heritage Museum; awards from the Academy of Western Artists; enshrinement in the Walkway of Western Stars, and more.  What began as a celebration of classic Western Music and an evening of hilarity has become a career, and that career has become a legend, one which, 40 years on, shows no signs of stopping or even slowing down much.
 
Ranger Doug, Too Slim, Woody Paul and Joey the Cowpolka King… 40 years on, “The Cowboy Way.”

combined_title: Comics Beyond Sight
description:
This exhibit covers a variety of creative approaches to comics visual accessibility, and by extension visual accessibility broadly. Those approaches range from multimedia (audio and textual descriptions) through multidimensional and emerging technologies strategies (3D printing, haptics, and screen-based mobile touch interfaces). It demonstrates that comics can be made accessible. Learn about the international efforts of innovators in the realm of comics accessibility for those who are blind or have low vision, assembled by the Accessible Comics Collective at San Francisco State University (SFSU) with the expertise of blind access professionals. 

Emily Beitiks was the accessibility lead for the content creation of the exhibit. She is the co-director for the San Francisco Disability Cultural Center (the first civically funded disability culture center on the planet!), and prior to that, the director of the Longmore Institute on Disability. 

Nick Sousanis (SFSU), the lead creative organizer of the exhibit, is a Detroit native and was the first person to draw his dissertation in comics format, subsequently published as the graphic novel Unflattening.

View the exhibit anytime the Hatcher Library is open, and join us for an opening presentation on Friday, October 2nd, 1:00pm - 4:00pm.

Celebrate the centennial of the iconic 1926 “Down in Ann Arbor Town” map by exploring the colorful history, campus traditions, and detailed artistry that made it possible. Created by Jessie Horton Koessler (Class of 1901) to help fund the Michigan League building for women, this celebrated map provides a fascinating view into 1920s campus life and the women who shaped it. Through three distinct exhibit sections, journey from the campus history that led to the map’s creation to a broader look at early 20th-century pictorial mapmaking.

While enjoying the exhibit, pick up a scavenger hunt at the Clark Library desk that will inspire you to notice whimsical details in the maps discussed. Return your scavenger hunt at the desk for a small prize, while supplies last.

Join the curators — Ava Pustulka (’28) and Anna Rohl, map curator at Clark Library — for a presentation on September 24 (https://myumi.ch/X8y3r), where they will share the research that went into creating the exhibit.

description:
Visit the Hatcher Gallery Exhibit Room to see historical materials that illustrate women’s changing relationship with food, cooking, and technology during the heady decade of the 1920s, sandwiched between WWI and the Great Depression. This exhibit features materials from the Janice Bluestein Longone Culinary Archive, as well as select items from the Art, Architecture, and Engineering Special Collections and the Transportation History Collection.

As America rang in a new decade in the 1920s, cookbook authors and appliance manufacturers stood ready to offer the newly emancipated and forward-thinking American woman a vision for her future, a vision that would be scientifically  grounded, speedy enough to make time for leisure as well as housework, and guaranteed to bring fun to that most humdrum of chores: planning and preparing meals for a family three times a day, 365 days a year.

event_subtitle: Contemporary Visions in Native American Art
description:
Join us at Matthaei Botanical Gardens for an art exhibit by Justin Johnson Nodagwzëwêk gi gdankobthëgnenanêk (our ancestors are heard): Contemporary Visions in Native American Art.  September 29 - November 15, 2026.

Artist Bio

“Bozho, Justin Johnson nde zhnëkas, Eau Claire ndë wtthbya. Mshiké ndodem minė Bodéwadmi ndaw.” (“Hello, my name is Justin Johnson, I come from Eau Claire. My clan is turtle and I am Potawatomi”). 

My name is Justin Johnson, Native name Thitthishkewé. I’m a visual artist whose work is deeply shaped by my Potawatomi heritage. Raised in Coloma, Michigan, my artistic path began in childhood and continued through grade school and high school, eventually leading to me studying at Kendall College of Art & Design for four years. My art is a reflection of both personal expression and cultural tradition, honoring the interconnectedness of people, animals, land, and spirit. Guided by intuition, ancestral knowledge, and the natural world. I’m always seeking new ways to tell stories through my work. My drawings are inspiration from tribal stories, culture, and values that have been passed down through generations. I have collaborated with the Pokagon Band on numerous projects, including traditional storybooks and illustrations. Aswell as permanent collections at the Pokagon Band Administration Building and the Pokagon Health Services building, and artwork featured in the Four Winds Casino gift shop. Some other projects and exhibtions that I’ve participated in would be the Native American exhibition at the Krasl Art Center and a featured as the cover artist with a six-page article in PAN-O-PLY magazine. My murals can be found at the Grand Rapids Public Museum, the Edwardsburg (Cass County District) Library, and the Buchanan District Library. Currently, I’m collaborating with Northwestern University on a new mural for their football stadium. Through diverse body of work, my work continues to share the stories, values, and traditions of his heritage with a wide audience.

Artist Statement

My work is deeply rooted in my culture, which shapes both my perspective and my creative process. We see ourselves as part of the Earth, not separate from it—every act, every gesture, is an exchange. When we take, we give. This relationship is woven into the art I make, which follows the tradition known as Woodlands Style, or Legendary Style. It’s not the invention of any one person. It has been handed down, shaped by countless hands and stories over generations. This style is often described as “x-ray” painting. With vivid colors and layered lines, I try to reveal the inner spirit of animals, plants, and people—sometimes physical, sometimes spiritual. There’s a rhythm to it that still echoes the Great Lakes region: bold, luminous, and full of life. Each piece is a story that’s been told and retold, woven across time, just like the spirits that guide us. As an artist, I try to reflect these values in everything I do. Even when we drift from the old ways, our spirit keeps us connected. My work is a reminder—a visual invitation to reconnect, to live more intentionally, and to honor the balance and respect that our traditions teach.

description:
From September 2025 through December 2026, Stamps Gallery is partnering in a curatorial collaboration with two Southeast Michigan-based, artist-run project spaces led by Stamps alumni: C.Y.N.K. Studios, directed by Sally Clegg (Lecturer III and Student Exhibition Coordinator, MFA ’20) and Abhishek Narula (MFA ’20); and Sometimes Space, directed by Nathan Byrne (Lecturer I, MFA ’21). Each space hosts dozens of artists annually for exhibitions, performances, and events, fostering experimental work and building community. For this project, Byrne, Clegg, and Narula have been commissioned to reimagine the pillars on Division Street that flank the gallery. In response, they’ve curated six artists to create new work for the pillars over three cycles:

Phase 1 (September 12 - December 12) artists: Amelia Burns (Cranbrook MFA ’23) and Erin McKenna (MFA ’20)
Phase 2 (January 12 - August 12) artists: Sally Clegg (MFA ’20) and Kim Karlsrud (MFA ’20)

Phase 3 

Curated by Sometimes Space: Abhishek Narula (entry pillar)
Curated by CYNK Studios: Nathan Byrne (courtyard pillar)

Artist Statements/Bios

Abhishek Narula, Compressions 
Compressions is an installation comprised of 416 industrial-grade zip ties, cinched around the entry pillar of the Stamps Gallery. The pillar measures roughly 110 inches in circumference, requiring two ties per row to wrap around it, resulting in 208 rows. The humble zip tie, typically used to hang and bind other material, is relegated to its functional properties rendering it unprepossessing and easily dismissed. The zip tie in this installation, instead serves as an object of aesthetic possibility, pulling it out of its usual background role to become the work itself. The resulting composition is a proposal to dwell, to slow down, and to simply see the pillar.

Abhishek Narula is an artist, designer, and educator who works across sculpture, installation, sound, and video. His practice takes the form of interventions, working with what is already present. He reorients and disrupts objects and sites in order to open up formal possibilities and poetic experiences within the familiar. He is influenced by physical and digital infrastructural systems that sustain modern life and culture. His work treats this ambience itself as raw material for aesthetic inquiry, exploring themes of labor, precarity, temporality and the sublime. Narula earned his MFA in Studio Art from the University of Michigan Stamps School of Art & Design and his MS/BS in Electrical Engineering from the Georgia Institute of Technology. His work has been exhibited at national and international venues such as the Ammerman Center for Arts and Technology, Science Gallery Detroit, Speculum Artium Media Festival in Slovenia, New Media Caucus (NMC), WaveFarm, The Boulder Public Library, The Hyde Park Art Center, Sector 2337 Art Gallery & Printing Press, Tangible Embedded Interaction (TEI), International Symposium of Electronic Arts (ISEA), among others. He is a Robotics Systems Designer and Lecturer in the Robotics Department at the University of Michigan. Website / Instagram

Nathan Byrne, Equally To Be Loved
Equally To Be Loved is an image / object scaled to and installed upon the courtyard pillar of Stamps Gallery. The image is of a spontaneous sculpture made in 2017 during the first day of an artist residency at the Recology San Francisco A.I.R. Program. The sculpture was constructed in a storage container studio using 14 discrete objects that were in his studio upon entry. For Byrne, this work embodies the energy and spirit of a studio at the start of a particularly fecund period of making. This work speaks to the artist’s interest in embodied experience of space, archival and site responsiveness, as well as his ongoing engagement with found materials. Byrne considers this project to be a far-flung sequel to his MFA thesis exhibition Equally Empty, which was shown at Stamps Gallery in 2021. Equally To Be Loved is the second line of the Buddhist mantra from which both titles are derived.

Nathan Byrne is an artist / educator / curator currently based in Detroit, MI. Through spatial and archive responsive projects, he reimagines, and explores within frameworks such as language, the passage of time, and contemplation. Intrigued by the potential of conveying phenomenal, transformative, and emotive states through materiality, process, and placement, he negotiates the pliability of the viewer’s encounters with objects and environments. Byrne holds an MFA in Art from the University of Michigan Stamps School of Art & Design and a BA in Studio Art and Art History from San Francisco State University. He has been a Lecturer at Stamps School of Art & Design since the Fall of 2022. His work is exhibited widely nationally and he is a recipient of the VSC Fellowship at Vermont Studio Center. He has been awarded numerous artist residencies including Anderson Ranch Arts Center, I-Park, KHN Center for the Arts, Prairie Ronde, Recology San Francisco A.I.R. Program, and Rockland Woods. event_title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism
combined_title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism: Nicola Barham, Curator
description:
The lifelike naturalistic bodies of Greek and Roman sculpture have been a source of wonder since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Italian Renaissance artist Vasari identified the ancient world as the time “when sculpture rose to its greatest height.” But close likenesses of the natural world are not the only visual products of the ancient past. This exhibition traces alternative visual trends in the ancient Roman world that today would be considered examples of abstraction. It focuses on monuments and motifs long pushed to the margins of our accounts of ancient art. Oversize arrangements of interlocking shapes pulsate in bold block colors from tombs, temples, and homes; stylized animals flicker into view, only to collapse once more into bright geometric arrangements; and artists adopt experimental shorthands for the depiction of space across media. Anticipating recent interests in color and form, the visual trends of antiquity emerge as far more varied than has long been told.

*Ancient Abstractions is on view from November 5, 2026, through February 28, 2027, during regular museum hours (Tuesday–Friday, 10:00 AM–4:00 PM, and Saturday–Sunday, 11:00 AM–4:00 PM; closed Mondays and university holidays.*

event_title: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”
combined_title: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”
description:
Changes over the course of the nineteenth century in how Americans voted, from voice vote to public ballot box to private voting booth, also saw changes in the material culture that surrounded voting. Ballots and ballot boxes, campaign pins and ribbons, blank lists and pre-printed party tickets, lanterns and banners–the creative forces of the American print industry filled the country’s cities and small towns with the ephemera of electioneering.

As you look at the items in this exhibit, think about what they tell us about how Americans in the past felt about voting, and about how voting felt. How did Election Days feel when they were full of parades and music and public drinking? What was it like to vote when everyone around you knew who you voted for? And, most of all, who counted as a voter, and who did the counting?

On view September 11-December 22, weekdays from 12-4 pm.

combined_title: Cosmo Whyte: Under the Quiet, Beyond the Eye
description:
Curated by Srimoyee Mitra

Stamps Gallery kicks off the fall 2026 semester with an ambitious mid-career survey of interdisciplinary artist Cosmo Whyte. Born and raised in Jamaica, Whyte completed a BFA from Bennington College and earned an MFA from the University of Michigan. He is currently a faculty member at the School of the Arts and Architecture, UCLA.

This exhibition brings together two central concerns that animate Whyte’s artistic practice: the archive, both personal and public, as a site of disturbance; and migration as a lived experience of refuge, refusal, and reinvention. In Whyte’s work, the archive is never static or neutral. Rather, it is a contested space where official histories encounter memory, inheritance, and the fragments of stories carried across generations. His practice moves within this charged interstitial terrain, between what has been recorded and what has been remembered, between institutional knowledge and embodied experience. Whyte invites the viewer to consider the fluidity of geographic borders and layered cultural identities that have persisted despite societal unrest caused by racial and socio-economic hierarchies across generations. In an era of intensified border politics and renewed debates over national identity, Whyte’s work offers a timely meditation on memory, movement, and belonging.

Presented with support from the U-M Institute for Humanities, the U-M LSA Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies, and the U-M Library.
